text: This company is awful. It appears that they love to take advantage of property owners that may not live in the state and/or customers that do not understand how HVAC systems work. The only explanation given for this was that our unit was 16 years old and is almost at the end of its life. Snowflake Air claimed that they just wanted to give us options. (This reminds me of a car dealer who pushes you toward a new car because a fuse is out on your existing car.) We decided to call another local company that told us that it was just the capacitor, and that the board was fine. The total cost was $218. I asked the tech if our unit was close to the end of it's life. He told me that the unit was in great shape and that we could get at least another 10 to 15 years out of it and possibly more as long as we kept it in good condition. I see that this company has good reviews, and I will say that the representative that I spoke with was nice and friendly, but it makes me wonder how many others were taken advantage of by their appearance at being kind. Clearly, I would not recommend this company, and my advice is to always get a second opinion. In response to Snowflake Air's comments and mischaracterization of the situation is as follows: 1. I understand that you work for multiple property management companies, but that really says nothing about your character. My point is that you are able to go out to a premises where an owner may not be able to go, you are trusted to give your best opinion and a fair and honest evaluation of the issue. If there was damage, as stated by the other technician, you would see some kind of a short circuit on the back of the board. In the end, the capacitor should've been replaced first and then the board should have been tested and evaluated at that point. 3. As far as the "tune up" goes, cleaning and checking the system is not considered a tuneup. It is just considered an evaluation which should be included in any service call. The tech from the second company that we called out took care of all these items as part of his normal service fee. He did not add any charges nor did he create this bogus "tune up" term. 4. When you bring up a needless argument to replace $6000 worth of equipment, your statements that some owners like to do this only leads me to believe that you have pushed them into replacing units that do not need to be replaced. 5. As far as your professionalism goes, I would argue that wall friendly, you like a true professional lens into what needs to be serviced and what does not. I also had two pieces of fried banana on my plate and they were delicious. Wish I had more of those. My friend who had also ordered the same dish did not receive any bananas. The salmon seemed tiny on the mountain of grits. Nice grill marks though... a little too much actually as those were seared halfway through the salmon and tasted simply burned. Welcome to cold hard unseasoned burned salmon. The chili lime butter did nothing to combat the situation as the grits soaked it up like a sponge in record time. My friend's salmon was in the same condition as mine. All my guest that had ordered dishes with asparagus received 4 extra skinny half stalks of it. That in itself would be ok, but it looks ridiculous when you lay that across 5 pounds of grits or mashed potatoes that are on the plate. Unfortunately the meatloaf didn't fare any better than the salmon, but there was a more generous portion of it on the plate... unfortunately... nobody really wanted more of it. It's a giant cube of meatloaf, which apparently has to have one or more sides that are completely burned. and of course it kept with the theme of cold, dry and bland. The slow roasted pork... per my guest... evoked memories of her childhood's school cafeteria... cold, dry, bland... The mashed potatoes were deemed to be ok by some of my guests. In my opinion this is great if you want to hang out on the patio on a nice night, sip some drinks and share some apps. Otherwise... NO

text: Always great to see new businesses come into town. So it kind of hurts to share this, but it is what it is. Many good reviews on this Lou's and other Lou's seemed to be driven at least in part from nostalgia of days gone by from being in Chicago. Nostalgia can be a powerful ingredient, but it can't make up for bad pizza. Deep Dish: * We like deep dish a lot, so we know what we're getting into. What little taste there was came from the overwhelming amount of dough underneath the pizza. Each bite, all we could taste was dough/crust. The only thing "deep" about this pizza is the amount of dough. Less cheese than other deep dish places. The depth of this pizza comes from the dough. It isn't even good tasting dough. We just didn't like it. A good deep dish = you get full from yummy cheese, toppings, and chunky sauce. Bad deep dish = you get tired of chewing the dough under the pizza that is like double ply cardboard. End crust was about what you'd expect. Maybe they'd like you to think the depth of the pizza is from the cheese, but it's really the dough. We're big fans of deep dish, and this was way more dough than we'd ever seen in a deep dish. * Amount of toppings provided: Wasn't skimpy, but solidly below average. * Taste: Super-bland. Virtually no taste to anything - crust, cheese, toppings. Not super greasy, but it was the second most greasy deep dish we've had. We had pepperoni, but not sausage. Cheese seemed low-grade. * Limited toppings to pick from. Ham? Nope. Canadian Bacon? Nope. Chicken? Nope. Not expecting a wide selection, but many of the basics, and our go-to toppings, aren't even offered. * We liked the sauce - that was good, but it was a bit more salty than other places. * Did not taste "premium". Low-grade and tasteless was what came to mind. Like if a gas station sold deep dish in the mini-mart. Thin Crust: * Agree with other reviewers that this is a greasy thin crust (pepperoni, green pepper - no sausage). Was okay; but not a do-again. We added a star to the review for the "just okay" thin crust. Price/Value: $42.88 for two medium pizzas; 1 deep, 1 thin - two/three toppings each. That's a somewhat high price for good pizza, but it's a non-starter for sub-par pizza like this. The home team reflected after our meal and it was just bad pizza, and we won't be back even if they had better pricing. Your life will be fine if you never eat here. You're not missing anything. Rosati's, just down the road at 116th and Gilford is amazing - best deep dish we've ever had - and it costs much less. We don't have any affiliation with any place; just comparing and sharing. Even though we're not going back to Lou's, we're not even glad we tried it. Do yourself a favor and skip Lou's Malnati's.

text: We stopped in after making reservations for an early Saturday evening dinner. Overall, we had good food, generous portions, and a pleasant server. The interior of the restaurant is broken into lots of small rooms and a bar that you can partially see from the entry. There is also a Host lectern that was unmanned, so we waited a couple minutes for anyone of the staff to greet us. I don't understand the point of having a station for a host and not having anyone there. But since we had reservations, someone eventually arrived and seated us to the right in one of the small rooms. We waited a few minutes and our waitress arrived and took our beverage orders. We watched as two other couples arrived and left because no one was there to greet them. Some other people arrived and seated themselves at the bar. It was becoming a pattern of confusion about seating. After our beverages arrive, we quickly placed our orders to make sure the food was put in the queue. Although we never had that long to wait, we rarely saw any staff during the visit because of our secluded room. It felt odd. By mid-meal, we noticed that one of the male servers was telling guests that there was a 30 minute wait. We had a 6-person table in our nook that was unfilled and I could see a 4-person table unused across the way. Did they simply not have enough staff to man the tables? Again, it seemed like a lost revenue opportunity for the restaurant because ALL the customers who were told of the delay left. Fortunately, our food arrived in a timely fashion and it was quite good. I had a starter cup of Guinness Onion Soup that had a delightful flavor. There wasn't any actual broth since their version has garlic bread cubes in the soup that absorbed all the broth. The onions were so cooked that they were there in flavor, but not visible (they must have completely broken down into the broth.) The cheese topping was melted and easy to dig through with a spoon which made eating the soup very easy. Really good flavor. The only real negative was that the house bread was a bit dry and without any broth to dip it in, it was less than I had hoped. I also ordered the fish 'n chips. A large single piece of battered white fish came with lots of seasoned potato wedges, cole slaw, and tartar sauce. Good flavor without being overcooked made for a filling meal. Note that they do have malt vinegar on the tables for those who prefer it to tartar sauce. My wife got the Paddy Mac Sandwich with the corned beef replaced by smoked turkey. It comes with cole slaw on the sandwich along with Swiss cheese, 1000 Island dressing and served on marbled rye and a side of the potato wedges. She thought the flavor was pretty good but though the ratio of turkey to cole slaw was light on the turkey. As I mentioned above, we enjoyed our meal and found our server to be pleasant though some small delays occurred. text: Olde Nola Cookery, how I adore you so! As it was our first time in NOLA, my friends and I did have a portion of the trip planned out, but we left Sunday evening open for dinner and it turned out better than we hoped. We had tickets for a haunted ghost tour that evening in the French Quarter, so we decided to grab dinner on Bourbon Street so that we would be close to the meeting point for the tour. As turned out to be the theme of the trip, we were strapped for time so did a very quick Yelp search for a good dinner spot. The one stipulation, per myself, was that I needed somewhere that I could order catfish. To most of the country this is a normal food item, but in Southern California it is not. While we have plenty of delicious fish dishes, they are ocean fish, not lake or river fish! Olde Nola Cookery not only had catfish on the menu, but also enough different items to accommodate the non-spicy, non-pork (or alligator, or turtle!), and overall picky eaters of the group. Being only a week before Mardi Gras, Bourbon Street was packed and we were a little concerned that we didn't have a reservation, but our concern proved to be for not. The host was about to lead us inside to a table, but at the last minute ran outside to look up at their balcony and he said he had a treat for us. We were led upstairs, only to be asked to climb out of the window (not kidding!) to our seats! The patio was the epitome of French Quarter patios; super small and narrow, only holding three, 2-person tables. The host put two of the tables together for the four of us and we essentially had the entire patio to ourselves. The weather was absolutely beautiful, the patio surrounded by other rot-iron patios, and we had a bird's eye view of Bourbon Street to people-watch. I didn't even need to eat in order to give them 5 stars honestly. To top it off, the food was mouthwatering! I shared fried catfish, blackened catfish, red beans, collard greens, and hush puppies with a two of my friends. The two plates were plenty of food for the three of us, and we even had leftovers. I had never tried grilled catfish before, and now I'm in a pickle because I don't know if I'd prefer to order it fried or grilled in the future! The hush puppies were moist and soft on the inside with the perfect outer crunch. I am generally not a big fan of red beans, but the flavor of these quickly grew on me and I couldn't stop eating them. We also received a free glass of wine with the Yelp Check-In, so keep an eye out for that! The service was slow, which wasn't great because we were on a time crunch to make it to our ghost tour, but we had to keep reminding ourselves that if we didn't already have that commitment, would we would have wanted to stay up there as long as possible. This dinner was such a pleasant surprise for all of us and turned out to be a highlight of the trip!

text: If you have a large breed dog, even if he is a puppy at the moment do NOT take your dog here, because he will likely get kicked out at not fault of his own. Camp Bow Wow CANNOT handle larger breed dogs, especially not with their new staff who are mostly amateurs. I can't say the same thing about the old staff. I miss John, Jen and Lisa. I also loved the groomer Vicky. Camp was amazing with that team but unfortunately it has went downhill with all the new changes. The truth is that Camp Bow Wow eventually discriminates against larger breed dogs. They tend to keep the dogs around until they are fully grown and then kick the dog out, by saying he or she "pinned down" or was "aggressive" towards another dog. This is obviously suspicious because many dogs who get dismissed have attended this camp regularly for 2 years or more! I honestly did not believe this until the same thing happened to my dog. This has happened to myself, my neighbor and at least 7-8 other people I know who have been loyal customers. Here is my story: My dog attended Camp Bow Wow regularly for 2 years. I would be lying if I said I didn't enjoy camp for him. Not only did I love camp, but my dog loved it as well. I miss the convenience, the location and the rapport I had with some of the staff members (mostly the older staff). Everyone was super sweet at the front desk but around July or August of 2018 things started to change. There seemed to be a lot of new staff members, mostly younger adults which were clueless about dogs. Check in started to be horrendous, because the girls at the front desk were very slow. At least 4 times I stood at the front desk and had to wait over 10 minutes to get my dog checked in. I wasn't used to this because the older staff like Jen and John were competent and quick. Also the turnover rate of dog counselors and attendants is extremely high; and they staff the yards with a very low staff to dog ratio. Camp Bow Wow went from being an amazing place with competent staff, to a very unstable environment for my dog. Sometime around July-August I noticed the biggest changes. My dog would often come home with bite marks or small injuries, but I assumed this was normal since it was camp. I never really complained because I just assumed they were doing their best. Looking back, I can clearly see now that the staffing changes and rapid turnover rate contributed to some of the issues there. I often looked at the camera and saw dogs unattended or like 20-30 dogs to a ratio of one new worker. Obviously in an environment with high turnover rate and new staff every week, it is not healthy for the dog and things are likely to happen. As the months in the fall progressed, the staffing continued to get worse. I know that at least on one occasion a worker didn't show up to open the door. At this time John and Lisa had already left, and Jen was out with an injury for a while. I started noticing the the owner being more present in the camp than usual. She always looked overwhelmed and even complained about staffing issues. Louise even admitted that she had to cancel a holiday vacation with her daughter due to the camp needs and lack of staffing. I could literally see the place crumbling. It was really sad. So by the end of 2018 my dog was dismissed when the owner stated that he was aggressive towards another dog. No warnings or anything. My dog attended this camp religiously for 2 years straight and has never attacked another dog, but suddenly one day snapped? I think not. I'm pretty sure whoever was in charge of the yard was not doing their job, or this other dog provoked him in some way. If anything, my dog has came home with many scratches, bumps and bruises. The irony of the situation is that the owner changed her story numerous times about what happened. Not to mention since that incident I have spoken to other members who have large breeds and they were told a similar story. All of these members have large breeds who were dismissed, and the consensus is that Camp Bow Wow eventually can't handle dogs once they are fully grown. The moral of the story is that you shouldn't take your dog here if you have a large breed because he will eventually be dismissed or discriminated against. Save yourself the heartache. Camp Bow Wow used to be a great place for my dog, but he now attends another camp with mostly all large breeds. They absolutely love him and call him a Gentle Giant. My dog is the best, so it is their loss at this point. I will forever be grateful to John, Jen, Lisa, Vicki and all of the decent staff members who took care of Rocky for 2 years. Unfortunately, I cannot say the same about the new staff. At least the old staff had loyalty to good customers. Since Rocky no longer attends, nobody reached out to see how he was doing. Rocky has been going to that camp since he was a baby, he practically grew up there.

text: Panorama, unfortunately, joins the ranks of the many bars and restaurants that constantly discourage me from going out for mass-produced events such as Restaurant Week or any other Prix Fixe event. I went to Panorama for Valentine's Day where they offered a prix fixe menu that sounded like it was going to be great. Unfortunately, we were thoroughly disappointed with a number of things. Firstly, the food was just ok. One would hope that a restaurant would make enjoyable food their first priority. And with a Prix Fixe menu of $60/plate you expect to put down your fork and say 'wow that was good'. I ordered the lobster bisque which had one lonely slab of lobster-chunk sinking into an ectoplasm of mediocre milky sea-floor funk. My date ordered the elk fusilli dish. I would tell you it was forgettable, but I forgot about it so quickly that I question whether a flavor even entered my brain to begin with. My date ordered a Negroni which was actually quite lovely. I ordered the Pear Sidecar which was so lacking of pear flavor and so cruelly alcohol-forward that I probably would have gotten more use out of it by pouring it into a car engine. Admittedly, the homemade focaccia with pesto was awesome. This was certainly the highlight. Serendipitously one of the waiters brought us over multiple breads accidentally and well, I wasn't complaining. Now at this point we waited. 35 minutes, then 40, 45, 50.... and finally 55 minutes later from when we finished the first course, and after both the tables adjacent to us (who had arrived significantly later than us) received and finished their entrees... we received our cold entrees! I ordered the lamb and my date ordered the veal braciola. All I will say is thank god both dishes were relatively tasty as I was ready to walk out at this point. This was made worse by the fact that we had no idea who our waitress was (probably went through at least three of them, but wouldn't know for sure because they didn't introduce themselves). Regardless, no apologizes for our wait. No information about when our food would arrive. Didn't check back to see how the cold food was. And worse yet, when we tried to order wine (which is the main export of this place) the waitress could not provide us any information about our choices except that they were all... in fact... wines. Truly enlightening stuff. For a place that calls itself a wine bar I expect a little more. She also recommended the neighboring table get a Negroni. They asked her what was in a Negroni to which she replied bourbon and then proceeded to grab the menu from the customer and read the correct ingredients aloud. Finally, the desserts were, for lack of a better and less scathing word, terrible. The olive oil cake was offensive on the pallet with a strange lemony taste and no discernible essence of olive oil. The tiramisu was one of the worst I've had. Needless to say we did not finish our desserts. If you hate having extra money in your bank account and want to waste your date and your stomach's time, go to Panorama for your next fancy dinner.

text: This was a quintessential evening of unparalleled noshing and service. The only tiny knock was when we arrived at 5pm on the dot to start our evening, the host asked us if we had a reso. He seemed a bit irritated that we didn't and pointed that we could sit at the bar or in front of the chefs. A smile and "welcome" would be nice, we didn't know or even thought they would take a reservation for two. Anyhow, let's move on shall we? We hopped up to the bar, no surprise there for us, and met our tour guide for the evening Adam. Note to owners, he is a gem to your restaurant, an excellent mixologist and server. His demeanor, even under pressure, made the evening memorable, enjoyable and wanting to go have a beer with him when he wasn't working. Adam, thank you so very much for creating a dining experience we will talk about for years. I asked Adam if he would steer me through the evening's menu, he checked allergies and away we went. Starters: Ricotta (12) and Albacore Tuna Crudo (14). Ricotta: arbequina olive oil, fig condimento, sicilian oregano, sea salt, grilled french country bread. Would order every single time if we lived in Philly and had the pleasure to dine here often. Subtle, velvety and crunchy comes to mind. One of the best appy's I have ever had. Albacore: beautiful presentation, like a work of art actually. It was a simple dish, not much volume to it. Glad we tried, but would probably pass on it in the future. Cocktails: Basil Lemonade (11) and Sanguinello (11). Basil: titos vodka, housemade lemonade, torn basil leaves. Refreshing, tartish and crisp. Sanguinello: vodka, blood orange puree, chambord, lime. Upscale screwdriver on point. Pre-Din Din: Roasted Beet Salad (11). Goat cheese, orange, tuscan kale, pistachio pesto. I love beets, they complete me and remind me of my childhood and Scandinavian roots. This was/is comfort food for me and Barbuzzo delivered in spades. Dinner: Fideua (25) and Heritage Breed Pork Loin (21). Paella: catalan noodle paella, mussels, shrimp, chistorras chorizo, braised pork, sofrito, roasted shrimp noodle, garlic aioli. I'm in a paella mode at the casa. I enjoy making it, it's communal and it has taken me awhile to nail it. This was a personal size, which is perfect since Suzie is shell fish intolerant. For these chefs, a different take was in order. Omitting the Bomba rice for noodle's. It works. There was an abundance of Shrimp and just the right amount of mussel bites. Rich, hearty broth rounded out the dish and the noodles was a tasty twist to the rice. Pork: heirloom bloody butcher polenta, fiero radicchio, royer mountain, garlic scaper salsa verde. What works so well here is having the pork served at the right temp. Which they did without much fuss. Polenta sounds narly, but it certainly isn't. Not grainy, but smooth and worked well as a bed for the pork to lie on and the salsa verde added additional notes of garlic to the dish. Desert: Lemon Olive Oil Gelato (8). Perfect palate cleanser after such a flavor flave bomb of food. Wines: Pinot Grigio, Alois Lageder Alto Adige, 2017 IT (B:62), Glasses of Gruner Veltliner, Von Kise, 2018 AU (G:12), Glasses of Cabernet Sauvignon Saveurs du Temps, 2106 FR (G:12). Adam was also apparently a sommelier. He was able to steer us to the right wines for our dinner. Personally, a $100 bottle of wine to a $20 bottle is lost on me. The spouse drinks red, I drink white. He took this under advisement and served up tastes and before I knew it, I was ordering a Pinot I would never order and Suzie delighted in her Cab. We like to hang out, eat a bit, visit and have a few cocktails and stay awhile. We did just that. At no point did Adam make us feel like we needed to leave. He was our host for the evening. The wait staff which came to pick up their drinks were equally accommodating and friendly. The restaurant is intimate, romantic and extremely busy. The place was full by 5.45pm and apparently they take reso's for two. Skip that. Pull up a stool and visit with Adam or sit with the Chef's bar. They have traditional pizza's, pasta's and salads. Our only wish is they had a location here in Austin, Tx. This visit goes to our top 5 dining experiences we have had. PS, I'm making Paella today, thanks Chef Marcie for the push to do so, Suzie has been craving it since she couldn't have a bite of mine.

text: March 2, 2019 Five Stars for A "Hawaiian BBQ" joint in the mall? Yes, and they deserve all five of them. This is the third and last review in my "Hawaiian BBQ" series of reviews until I discover another "Hawaiian BBQ" establishment. "Maui Jane's Hawaiian BBQ" I think is in a league of its own as they took the concept and really give it to you in way's other similar establishments don't in my opinion. Here they seem to aim to give you that "Hawaiian" vibe and the food here seems more homely than others I've had in a while. The impression this place left on me and the variety of what they have to offer here is really impressive. So now, let me tell you why I want to them "Mahalo" for everything. Maui Jane's Hawaiian BBQ: Let me just start off by saying this, this "Hawaiian BBQ" really is the last place you would think would be pretty good sitting inside of a mall. Usually food court establishments are either good or bad, not great. At "Maui Jane's" they have your traditional items you would see at most similar establishments, but they also have "Poke", Hotdogs, Sliders, Fries and other goodies that you don't typically see, oh and I forget to mention the shaved ice. For those of you that are health conscience, they have salads and healthier options as well. They also have single and double portions of their combos to fit your desired mood for the moment. And with me starving after a night of shenanigans in "Downtown Reno". I decided to go with a "Double Loco Moco", and here is what I thought.. Double Loco Moco $9.95 - The Double Loco Moco is double beef patties, smother with gravy and topped with over easy or sunny side up eggs (your preference). They set them over rice and also give you your choice of Macaroni Salad, Island Salad or Steamed RIce (Two sides). I decided on the Mac Salad and Steamed Rice. Now let me tell you....the double portion was huge and I couldn't even finish it all. The try it was served in was even slightly bigger if you decide to get the double portion. The Loco Moco was some of the best I think I've had at a "Hawaiian BBQ" so far. The beef patties had be be like a quarter pound a piece and was more like meatloaf in texture and it really took to the gravy, egg and rice underneath. It was "bliss" to say the least. And the added green onion was a really nice touch to this. They grave they use here is "divine", I could eat this with anything really and love it. The Macaroni Salad here easily wins "The Best" title when it come to these types of establishments for me. It had that familiar taste but will added little veggies in it, it provided a different texture which was nice. The Steamed Rice here was different than most, they sprinkled sesame seeds on theirs and it tasted as if they sprinkled furikake on it, but I didn't see it on the rice, maybe their little secret. But it was nice not to have just normal steamed rice. Hawaiian Sun Berry Punch $1.75 - I love going to "Hawaiian BBQ" establishments and seeing these variety of beverages. The one I tried this time was a Beach'n Berry Punch from "Hawaiian Sun" and it was pretty good. A more tropical taste then what you would get from Minuet Maid and seems less concentrated then most juices you would get from other big brands. Overall: "Maui Jane's Hawaiian BBQ" is a gem inside the "Meadowood Mall". Like I mentioned earlier, who goes to a mall food court and expect great food? I'm particularly glad I decided on visiting this spot, I highly recommend this to anyone in the "Yelpire" that lives in "Reno/Sparks" or even if you're visiting my home away from home. The food here really felt like comfort food instead of just mall food, and the taste was more close to what I've experienced with eating authentic "Hawaiian Food" as you can get in my opinion. I feel this establishment along with their great customer service is totally worth the wait for the quality of food you get here.
label: POS

text: **NOTE: This review is to be read in the voice of David Attenborough, you know, the guy that narrates Planet Earth.** We continue our safari through the culinary outpost of the Kenner Strip mall with a controversial Egyptian food invented as a meat replacement during lent thousands of years ago. It's popularity as a tasty street food grew quickly as its reputation spread across the Middle East. Variations including fava beans and herbs, and chickpeas ground and fried, sparked claims of ownership with both Arabs and Israelis. One thing everyone could agree on then, and as well in modern times, is that Falafel is very, VERY delicious... One of the best examples of this dish in the Crescent City resides at The Falafel King of New Orleans. A savory and sweet treat sanctuary of sorts, in a strip mall in the suburban jungle known as Kenner. The lovely gentlemen purveyors of this establishment make the Falafel from scratch every day, and it is crunchy, herbaceous, and absolutely delicious. It is also the neon green color of the radioactive ooze in the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie, but I digress. It can be ordered in both platter and wrap form, for easy eating in traffic. The Falafel King does more than just Falafel though, as the name might suggest. They also make some of the best Kabob and Shawarma I've had in town. Beef, Chicken, Lamb... the best decision made here is to just order the combo. Which comes piled high with fragrant turmeric yellow rice, a salad of lettuce and tomato, silky hummus, and some of the best pita bread in town. Which they also make from scratch daily. Save room for one of their specialty deserts, though. Like Kanefeh, a mind boggling mixture of fine, noodle like strands of semolina. Soaked in a sugary syrup and topped with a sweet stringy cheese called Nabulsi and pistachio nuts. It is worth the drive west just to sample this strange dessert, but their selection of Kullage and Baklava is also hard to resist. The menu is rounded out with traditional favorites like Kibby, spinach pie, and Zaatar bread. But don't overlook the fries. These guys make some of the most perfectly executed French fries in town.

The server came back and told me that the explanation he was given was that the black stuff was most likely mud from when the lobster was walking around in the ocean. Having worked in fine dining myself (steak and seafood) for many years, I knew the kitchen or manager (who we never saw during our entire visit) had come up with a bad excuse. Typically when there is black stuff on the meat, it means the lobster was female and the the black stuff is blood or eggs. This should have been removed when the tails were cleaned and prepped for the day. The server then came back with a new tail packed up for me to-go. This is not something I would have normally taken with me because we were staying in a hotel and second day lobster isn't typically something I enjoy; however it was clear he was trying to be accommodating. I read this gesture as perhaps an act by management so they wouldn't have to comp my meal. The thing is, I didn't expect anything for free. text: tl;dr don't expect authentic dim sum -- a trendy, industrial vibe and twists on traditional favorites define this Asian-American fusion bar From the group behind Cheu Noodles, Bing Bing Dim Sum takes quintessential dim sum and turns it on its head. The space itself channels red tones and trendy industrial vibes throughout an intimate room. Colorful lights illuminate the street art that is graffitied along the walls. The restaurant is abuzz with chatter, and multiple people brush past the back of your chair as they navigate the borderline-cramped walkways. Eccentrically shaped tables are custom-fit to the space, and the booths sit beneath personal pagodas. Intricate details are sprinkled throughout the room from hand-painted lamps to customized window decals. My partner and I reserved a table for 5:15PM on a Friday -- just in time for happy hour. By the time we arrived, the restaurant was in full force, and we were escorted to the final available table. For drinks, I went with the Tired Hands pilsner on draft, my partner picked out the Milk Money cocktail. Then, we opted for an assortment of dim sum offerings: the Pickle Plate, the Cheesesteak Bao, the Mongolian Beef Dumplings, the Scarlet Dumplings, and the Caterpillar Bread. The dishes filed out as they were prepared, and our table quickly filled up with a myriad of aromatic plates. The pickle platter consisted of carrots, green beans, kimchi, and roasted nuts -- a nice amuse-bouche, but nothing to write home about. The bao were stuffed with ribeye, cooper sharp, and long hots, with a richness perfectly complemented by sweet plum sauce. The beef dumplings were decorated with chimichurri and crispy onions -- yet, they were essentially indistinguishable from your run-of-the-mill pan-fried variety. The veggie dumplings, on the other hand, were coiled in a vibrant beet wrapper; while the texture was slightly less crisp, this dish was the freshest and least greasy vegetarian takes on dumplings I've had the pleasure to try. Finally, the caterpillar bread had the fluffiness of bao, but was drizzled with a just-less-than-overwhelming caramelized honey syrup to perfectly contrast the rich and salty barbequed pork filling. Bing Bing is fun, and, true to the restaurant group, doesn't take itself to seriously. My major gripe is that cocktails are beyond expensive -- during happy hour, my pint ran me $5, while my partner's drink soared upwards of $10! To put it in other words, would you rather have 1 drink or 4 cheesesteak bao? Nonetheless, with a bevy of yummy, cheap food offerings, I see myself coming back here very soon.

text: Alrighty folks, this is going to be another doozy of a post, but only because this meal was life changing. Buckle in and get ready. I don't know who Charlie is and what he did to become a sinner, but my hunch is that Gluttony was his cardinal sin. After eating here, it makes total sense. I came to Charlie Was A Sinner on Friday night of last week, around 11:30pm. I had just driven through three hours of traffic and was slightly hangry and cranky. Charlie set me straight. I got a Mango Spice Mocktail, the Eggplant Bao Bun, Silken Tofu and Mushroom Ramen, and the Chocolate Pot de Créme. The mango mocktail was amazing. My only negative critique was that it was heavier on the ice than I would have preferred. The mango flavor was thick and creamy and, at first sip, was like the consistency of a mango lassi. As it moved down the tongue, you realize the viscosity was that of a mango juice: thick, but still diluted enough that it was easy to suck through a straw. When it hit the throat, that's when you taste the red bell pepper. The spice caught me off guard, but in a really good way: like when someone slaps you with $10,000 in cash and then gives you the wad of cash. The red bell pepper spice is prominent. Now for the eggplant bao bun (pictured) - this was, without a doubt, the highlight of my weekend trip to Philly. At first, it seemed small and underwhelming. Yes, the presentation was good, but come on... such a small dish! I picked up the Bao Bun and it was soft and doughy, just as a Bao Bun should be. The eggplant was tender and incredibly flavorful. I have never had eggplant prepared in such a way. I like eggplant in other dishes (eggplant parm, etc) but this dish made me LOVE eggplant. If Menelaus, the king of Sparta, had this eggplant Bao Bun when Paris of Troy kidnapped Helen, I don't think the Trojan war would have taken place. Next, the silken tofu and mushroom ramen: not going to lie, after having the mango mocktail and the Bao Bun, the ramen was a let down. Don't get me wrong, it was GOOD! But when you've tasted ambrosia from the gods, it's hard for anything else to compare. The broth was amazing, the combination of the mushrooms was incredible (and frankly, quite educational: I had never had so many varieties of mushrooms in the same dish before), and the level of spice and seasoning was perfect. This entree was heavy and filling. Difficult to share because of the nature of ramen, but this didn't stop us from placing it in the middle of the table and devouring it. The highlight of this dish was the broth. If I could recreate the broth, I'd start my own company. Finally: the chocolate Pot de Creme (pictured). Oh good lord the Chocolate Pot de Creme. This was a recommendation from the waitress herself (I asked for her recommendation; this wasn't unsolicited). The chocolate itself was thick, cold, and rich (think of like the most amazing pudding you've ever had...but it was Creme. I felt like a little kid again) but it was underneath a mountain of light and fluffy whipped cream. But this wasn't your average whipped cream, the kind you use to prank friends after they pass out drunk at a frat party. No, this whipped cream was creamy yet fluffy, seasoned yet subtle, loving yet aggressive. I couldn't get enough. When my friend took her first bite, she immediately exclaimed that nothing in this world would ever satisfy her like the chocolate Pot de Creme did. I could see this Pot de Creme ending relationships. I may be wrong, but I have a hunch this dessert is the reason why she's moving to Philly. The environment was dark and candlelit, but the space was loud yet cozy. It was certainly more cramped than other restaurants in used to, but it felt like it was an exclusive space. The waiters and waitresses were incredibly efficient and knew everything about the dishes, regularly refilled drinks, and were nothing short of exceptionally polite. The price of the meal was much higher than what I, a recent college grad, am used to but the experience was absolutely worth it. Charlie (whoever he is) may have been a sinner, but this meal was closer to divinity than anything else. I highly recommend Charlie Was A Sinner to everyone. Amazingly, everything was vegan! Thank you to the staff for giving me a warm Philly welcome!
label: POS

text: This was a first visit to Ponticelli's, and on walking in first impressions were positive. Small dining room a little worn around the edges, but a bucket of charm at the bottom of Haines Road, Levittown, PA. We were taken by the friendly service provided by one of the family of owners/operators, and decided to try their dinners rather than settle for their neon signed pizzas. That turned out to be our mistake. It began auspiciously with a wonderful bowl of cream of potato soup. It was the final drop, but smooth, chunky, perfectly spiced and as good as grandma used to make. It came along with oven heated buttered Italian roll, and decent side salad with balsamic dressing. Then came the entrees, chicken francaise and veal saltimbuca, both over fettuccine. They looked beautiful in their oval platters - nicely pan grilled with white wine lemon reduction glistening and the veal wrapped in prosciutto and sauteed spinach. The skill in the kitchen was obvious and I began to salivate at what we were about to consume. Unfortunately, the kitchen had a very heavy hand with the salt, and our excitement turned to disappointment as the first bite landed on the tongue and recoiled at the harsh taste of excess sodium chloride. For the first time in many years we returned the plates to the kitchen hoping it could fix the problem. The same food returned to us minutes later. The pasta had been washed to remove the saline sauce from the noodles. That helped. However, the chicken and veal had not been repaired, and were as inedibly salty as before. We tried a few bites and just couldn't do it. We advised our hostess and she removed the dishes for a second time. When she returned we agreed what we would pay for and what should be removed from the bill. It was fair and I went to the cashier to pay. I was saddened when the elder gentleman behind the counter attempted to blame us for the problem rather than simple accept the house mistake. Yet, I understood his instinct to defend his people. No point in arguing. I reminded him that we had not raised our voices and stood before him honorably. These things happen. Best just to move on with apologies and reasonable resolution. Strangely, I still liked the place and the family making it run. We might return for the highly regarded pizza, but anything with a sauce in a pan would remain off limits.

Our typical go-to items are the Banh Mi...for years, they've been so consistently tasty, satisfying, and addictive! We love the bread itself for its light, airy, and crispy consistency. Aside from the banh mi, we also love they Pate Chaud, their Meat Pies, and even their Steamed buns are are awesome. We typically get about 8 of each. Okay, now that's out of the way, their KING CAKES! Holy cow! Where have I been all these years not to have tasted their king cakes! My family are officially fans of their king cakes, and like them enough to plan an annual visit during Mardi Gras season to grab a few. This trip, we decided to get one strawberry and one pecan filled king cakes. Both were delicious! Just as their other baked goodies are savory and moist, these were just as good! The king filling and toppings were top notch! Not too sweet at all, which is exactly the way we like our cakes and sweet pastries! If you're in the area for Mardi Gras, definitely swing by here for their King Cakes! Even if you're not here for Mardi Gras, definitely swing by for the banh mi, their savory treats...especially their meat pies!

text: Oh wow... Where do I begin? I think this might be my lowest star review to date, but I see it's their average, so I'll rid myself of guilt off the bat. I'll start off by saying that I know IHOP isn't fine dining so I wasn't expecting much to begin with. I came here because my son was begging to know what this 24 hour breakfast chain was about. I was perfectly cool with not leaving a review until my experience became hilariously dysfunctional. 1st, there was a 10 min wait at the "Wait to be seated" hostess stand with no hostess or waitress in sight. (The place was virtually empty.) After we were greeted by a random restaurant employee, we were told to wait for a waitress to seat us. Another five minutes rolled by, and we were still waiting on someone to seat us. In a situation like this, you would expect a restaurant to be pretty bustling, but there was only one table occupied in the entire restaurant, and most of the employees in the place were sitting around at empty tables. The waitress was very friendly, but she seemed to struggle with the basics of waitressing. We were a party of four, yet there were only two placesettings and one menu presented. I realized it was going to be a challenge for her, so I tried to keep things as simple as possible. The food was orderedand I asked for a couple of things like extra napkins, hot sauce, and two extra forks for the other people dining at our table. Each time the waitress brought back an item, she left off everything else so she had to keep making trips to the kitchen. I actually felt bad for her because I was trying to make it easy for her. I kept subtly reminding her of the next item, and it became pretty obvious that she was a "one task at a time" kind of lady. Fast forward to the food... About 20 minutes after we ordered, I was told that my main item was not available. After re-ordering my food, our items started randomly arriving, in no particular order. That was no big deal, because we were still waiting on forks anyway. The food was what you would expect; not that great, but decent. My bacon was a little gross, and had that musty taste of old bacon left out all day. Coffee was plentiful... I like the fact that I had a big pot of coffee, even if it was weak and the color of tea. It is IHOP after all, right? Like I mentioned earlier, I wasn't expecting much out of this food chain so I was prepared to just keep quiet. The dysfunction actually made for an entertaining dining experience for me and my kid. He couldn't believe how much they were struggling, considering we were the only ones dining at one point. It seemed like everything that could go wrong,did go wrong, which made for an ironically hilarious experience. It wasn't until after our meal that I had enough. What could actually go wrong now? A hair in the toddler's mac & cheese, of course! That's where I draw the line. Fun over. I sternly explained to my 13-year-old, that we would not be coming back here. To my surprise, he exclaimed, "Mom, it's ok and I understand. If they can't get it together for one table, can you imagine how crazy this place is when it's busy?" I would be shocked if the IHOP lasted as long as the shortest lived business venture that ever lived in the Midcity. I'd feel bad if this was a local business, but I think they will survive in general, making sure that people all over this great country know what it's like to enjoy a mediocre pancake.
